extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of American journalism history; general readers interested in colonial press
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes standards, practices, and functional criteria that defined colonial American newspapers (c.1690-1765), including editorial norms, business model, distribution, content types, and relations with government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary functions of the newspaper
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers served chiefly for reporting on public affairs and furnishing entertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes a dual role: informing the public about government and public affairs while also providing essays, poetry, and other amusements to 'lighten their pages.' Examples: Pennsylvania Gazette's aim to be an 'agreeable and useful Entertainment.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial practice: rarity of formal editorials
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal editorial pages and explicit editorial statements were uncommon in colonial papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors more often used contributed letters, signed pseudonyms, extracts from books, or occasional pointed remarks; Benjamin Franklin printed very little formal editorial comment (exceptions include his remarks after Governor Burnet's obituary and on 'the present disunited state of the British Colonies').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contributed letters, pen-names, and extracts for public discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of public affairs was typically carried on through contributed letters or essays, often signed by fanciful pen-names, and by extracts from books and pamphlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bold papers printed many such articles; the New York Weekly Journal filled with political articles in its fight with the Cosby administration; Boston Independent Advertiser printed political papers of Samuel Adams. Some of these pieces were written by editors themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial openness vs. editorial control (columns policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common doctrine held that publishers should open columns to all controversialists (especially if paid), but some editors resisted filling papers with private altercations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many editors adopted a policy of open columns; Franklin objected, saying his newspaper was 'not a stagecoach, with seats for everyone' and offered to print pamphlets for private distribution rather than fill his paper with disputes. Thomas Fleet professed neutrality—an impractical ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pamphlet as the preferred vehicle for extended argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Pamphlets were considered more appropriate than newspapers for setting forth important or extensive views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers were small and could not accommodate long eighteenth-century arguments; individuals had more freedom in their own pamphlets. Pamphlets were frequent, often 'immoderate and irresponsible'—Franklin published plans (e.g., currency reform) as pamphlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertainment and 'feature' material as filler and value
rubrics_metrics.description: Essays, poetry, and 'feature' material were used to entertain and fill space when news was scarce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some editors treated such material as mere 'filler' (e.g., New-England Courant devoted itself to amusing essays); Samuel Keimer inserted extracts (encyclopedia) when lacking news; printers explicitly promised agreeable entertainment to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising as chief profit margin
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising represented the primary source of profit for newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By mid-eighteenth century successful papers filled multiple pages with merchant and trader announcements; ads varied from two lines to a column, mostly under ten lines. Typical ad categories: runaways (slaves, apprentices), merchandise lists, lotteries, quack medicines, vendues, real estate, sailings, theatrical bills. First paid ad noted was for lost anvils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising format and typographic evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Early ads were single-column, ordinary body type with little display; over time separators, rules, and small cuts were introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initially no cut-off rules separated ads; later additions included rules, English (14 point) lines, small rude cuts of ships/horses/runaways, varied type-sizes (e.g., New York Post-Boy up to great primer), and occasional double-column prominent ads (example Thomas Trowell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising rates and payment conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard advertising charges were three to five shillings for first insertion (<10 lines) and one to three shillings for subsequent insertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prices existed alongside barter/alternate payments; subscription prices and ad charges must be read in context of depreciated currencies and scarcity of coin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation and subscription pricing (contextualized by currency depreciation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subscription prices and circulation figures must be interpreted relative to depreciated currencies and local accounting units (e.g., Spanish dollar 'computed this year at £4 Old Tenor').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Printed subscription rates ranged six to twenty-four shillings a year (ten/twelve shillings common); some accepted fuel or provisions in payment. Circulations typically a few hundred to a thousand; Boston average ~600 mid-century; perhaps ~5% of white families received a weekly paper but pass-along made readership larger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution: use of carriers and postriders
rubrics_metrics.description: Local delivery by carrier (often the apprentice/printer's boy) and inter-town transport by official postriders were standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carriers delivered damp sheets, solicited small New Year's gifts with 'carrier's addresses' (an institutionalized annual custom). Postriders carried bundles between towns (not as part of the mails) and their dramatic arrivals were public events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postal system relations and postage policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Printers often served as postmasters; newspapers were customarily carried free from office to office, but fees were charged for home delivery and rival publishers could be discriminated against.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Queen Anne’s Postoffice Act (1711) the post improved slowly; Franklin and Hunter (1753) extended routes and, in 1758, required subscribers to pay postage of ninepence sterling per year for every fifty miles (or fraction) carried by postrider—even as 'papers exchang’d between Printer and Printer' were to be carried gratis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of inter-printer exchanges for news supply
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors relied on receiving other papers and letters by ship or postrider to fill news columns; 'exchanges' with other printers were vital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local news was held in low estimation; delays or failures of exchanges/posts often led to scarcity of news and supplements; complaints about late post arrivals are recorded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial vulnerability due to delinquent subscribers
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonpayment by subscribers was a chronic and serious problem for printers' finances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Few subscribers paid in advance; many were in arrears (examples: Zenger's subscribers 'upwards of seven years'); appeals to delinquents were common and sometimes desperate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of personal controversy and neutrality norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Some early printer-editors attempted to avoid publishing material that attacked particular persons, but neutrality proved impractical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thomas Fleet declared he would not publish anything concerning a particular person's character or interest, but few papers adhered to such creeds; controversial material was common and often partisan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of imagery and the early newspaper cartoon
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual devices such as cartoons and cuts were used to reinforce editorial points and capture popular imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Franklin's divided-snake cartoon ('Join, or Die') accompanying his editorial on colonial disunity—recognized as the first American newspaper cartoon and widely reproduced; later papers used small cuts (ships, horses) in advertising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper–government relations and censorship pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers negotiated a tense relationship with colonial authorities; censorship threats and official reprisals constrained outspoken criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers often printed official documents impartially and avoided editorial comment to reduce reprisals; examples include assemblies forbidding printers from publishing certain documents and reprimands of printers for 'presumption.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactics of resistance to government taxation (Stamp Act responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Faced with the Stamp Act's requirement to use stamped paper and taxes on advertisements, printers adopted combined tactics: protest coverage, mourning issues, suspension, and defiance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Printers printed full accounts of legislative protests, mob stories, and destruction of stamped paper; some published defiantly without stamps, argued legal/practical invalidity of the Act, suspended publication to 'deliberate,' or used mourning (black rules) before suspension; some evaded the law by omitting the imprint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content selection hierarchy: foreign news vs. local news
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication prioritized news from abroad; local news was often considered of low value and less relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors depended on ship and post arrivals for foreign news; local news was not highly prized—hence the reliance on exchanges between printers to obtain content and frequent reprinting of foreign accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common advertisement content categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Colonial advertisements repeatedly covered specific social/economic items: runaways, auctions, lotteries, theatrical bills, goods (tea, molasses), books, and quack medicines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: runaway slaves/apprentices, lotteries funding colleges, Bohea tea staples, quack 'Excellent Medicine' copy listing many ailments cured; theatrical ads more common in Charleston and later in Philadelphia/New York.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural institution: carrier's addresses and annual versified appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: The printer's apprentice (carrier) traditionally delivered New Year's 'carrier's addresses'—versified appeals to subscribers for small gifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These addresses recounted events of the year in doggerel and solicited small gifts; the custom persisted well into the nineteenth century.
